opus-5.5.text:
Supply is something we think about constantly, because you can have the best architecture in the world, but if you can't get wafers, packaging, and memory, you don't have a business.

A few things work in our favor. First, we made some deliberate architectural choices early on. A lot of the industry is fighting over the same scarce resources: leading-edge capacity, advanced packaging like CoWoS, and above all HBM. HBM is incredibly constrained right now, and the big players have locked up much of that supply. Our approach with digital in-memory compute keeps a lot of the working data close to the compute, on-chip in SRAM, so we're not as dependent on HBM as a traditional GPU-style design. We pair that with more commodity memory like LPDDR for capacity, which has a much broader and more resilient supply base. That wasn't only a performance decision. It was a strategic one about where the bottlenecks would be.

Second, we use a chiplet-based design. Smaller dies give better yields, more flexibility in how we put products together, and we're not betting everything on one giant reticle-sized die coming out perfectly.

Third, relationships. We've worked closely with our foundry and packaging partners for years, well before inference became the hot topic. In this industry, being a reliable, committed customer before the crunch matters. We forecast carefully, we commit early, and we keep those partners informed about where we're headed.

That said, I'd be lying if I said we're immune. Everyone in the semiconductor ecosystem is feeling pressure, and as demand ramps, a startup has to be very disciplined about capacity planning. We're not going to win by outbidding hyperscalers for the scarcest components. We'll win by designing around those constraints, and that's been part of our thinking from day one.

r001.rationale: The response discusses careful forecasting and early commitments, but does not say D-Matrix’s relatively small demand makes TSMC more able to supply it.

r002.rationale: It does not mention using older TSMC process nodes or connect process-node choice to supply access.

r003.rationale: It says the SRAM-based design makes D-Matrix less dependent on constrained HBM and frames that choice as a way to design around supply bottlenecks.

r004.rationale: CoWoS is named as a scarce resource, but the response does not say D-Matrix avoids using it or connect such avoidance to securing supply.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Supply is probably the question I spend the most time on, candidly, because the architecture we build is only as good as our ability to actually ship it.

Let me break it down into the two pieces that matter for us: silicon and memory.

On the silicon side, we're a fabless company. We work with TSMC, and like everyone else we're competing for capacity at advanced nodes. The honest answer is that a startup never gets the same priority as Nvidia or Apple. But there's a nuance that works in our favor. Our Corsair product is built as chiplets on a mature, well-understood process rather than being a giant monolithic die on the bleeding edge. Smaller dies mean better yield, and better yield means we get more usable product out of every wafer we're allocated. We also don't need the very newest node to deliver our value, because our advantage comes from the in-memory compute architecture, not from being first on the latest process. That gives us flexibility that a company chasing peak FLOPs on a monolithic die simply doesn't have.

Then there's advanced packaging, which is actually the tighter constraint across the industry right now. CoWoS capacity is the bottleneck everyone's fighting over. We made a deliberate choice early on to avoid HBM, and that decision does double duty. HBM is in extremely short supply, with the memory vendors essentially sold out to the hyperscalers for the next couple of years. By building our design around SRAM-based compute and using commodity LPDDR for capacity, we sidestep that whole fight. We're not standing in line behind Nvidia for HBM3E, and we're not standing in the same line for the most constrained packaging flows either.

The third piece is planning discipline. We've placed long-lead orders well ahead of customer demand, which is uncomfortable for a startup from a cash perspective, but it's the only way to be credible with a hyperscaler or a large enterprise. When they ask whether we can deliver thousands of cards in a given quarter, you need to already have wafer starts committed. Our investors understood that this capital would be spent on inventory, and that's part of what the recent rounds were for.

Now, I don't want to be naive about it. If the memory market stays this tight through 2027, even commodity DRAM pricing becomes a factor, and we'll feel that in our bill of materials. And there's always a risk that a large player locks up capacity in a way that squeezes smaller vendors. But I'd rather be in a position where our dependencies are on the more abundant parts of the supply chain than where everyone else is fighting. We designed for that on purpose, and so far it's holding up.

r001.rationale: The response says smaller dies improve yield per allocated wafer, but does not say D-Matrix’s relatively small demand makes TSMC more willing or able to supply it.

r002.rationale: It says the product uses a mature process rather than the bleeding edge, does not require the newest node, and that this gives the company flexibility in securing supply.

r003.rationale: It explains that avoiding HBM lets the company sidestep the HBM supply shortage and the competition for that memory.

r004.rationale: The response identifies CoWoS as a bottleneck and says the design avoids constrained packaging flows, but it does not clearly state that D-Matrix avoids CoWoS technology.

astra-6.text:
We think about supply in two parts: access to manufacturing capacity and the components our architecture depends on. You have to plan capacity well ahead of demand and work closely with your manufacturing and packaging partners. That’s an ongoing effort, especially as the industry scales.

Our architectural approach helps because we’re not dependent on high-bandwidth memory in the same way that conventional GPUs are. We bring computation close to memory, which gives us a different supply-chain profile. It doesn’t eliminate supply risk—you still need wafers, packaging, and other components—but it reduces our exposure to one of the constraints in AI infrastructure.

So I’m optimistic, but I wouldn’t say supply is something you can take for granted. You have to align customer demand with capacity commitments and keep executing.

sol-6.1.text:
We think about supply in two parts: manufacturing capacity and the memory supply chain. You have to plan for both well ahead of demand and work closely with your partners, because you can’t turn on semiconductor capacity overnight.

One advantage of our architecture is that we don’t depend on high-bandwidth memory, or HBM. We use SRAM-based digital in-memory computing, which reduces our exposure to that particular supply bottleneck. That doesn’t eliminate supply risk—we still need wafers, packaging, and testing capacity—but it gives us a different supply profile.

So I’m confident in our approach, but I wouldn’t say supply is something you can take for granted. The key is aligning customer demand with capacity commitments early enough to deliver.
